hypotheses.name: Santorini (Thera)

proposed_by.work: The Volcanic Destruction of Minoan Crete, Antiquity 13

proposed_by.who: Angelos Galanopoulos and J. V. Luce
proposed_by.work: Galanopoulos (1960) and Luce, The End of Atlantis (1969), as listed by Atlantipedia

hypotheses.argument: The eruption of Thera, dated about 1600 BCE, destroyed the town of Akrotiri and, with its tsunami and ash, is said to have hit Minoan Crete. Proponents read that disaster, and the end of a sea power, as the memory behind Plato's sunken island.

fits.how: The BBC reports new evidence that Crete was hit by a massive tsunami at the same time Minoan culture disappeared; proponents read that as the sudden loss Plato describes.

conflicts.how: The eruption is dated to about 1600 BCE, roughly a thousand years before Solon, not 9,000. Robert Ballard says he does not think Santorini was Atlantis because the eruption date does not match Plato's.
Santorini is in the Aegean, inside the Mediterranean, not in front of the Pillars of Heracles (our legends.json 'against' note).

tests.what: Excavation of Akrotiri
tests.result: A Bronze Age town buried by the eruption was found. The dig does not test any link to Plato's text.
tests.evidence: Excavations starting in 1967 at the Akrotiri site under Spyridon Marinatos have made Thera the best-known Minoan site outside Crete.

replies.what: Santorini is a logical model for a catastrophe, but not Atlantis, because the dates do not coincide.

hypotheses.standing_reason: It is the real event most often named as a possible seed of the story, taken seriously by some classicists and archaeologists, while most scholars still read the dialogues as invented (National Geographic).
hypotheses.date_of_the_proposed_event: about 1600 BCE (the date itself is still argued)

sources.title: BBC News, The wave that destroyed Atlantis (2007)

hypotheses.notes: Wikidata Q129296 ("Santorini") property P625, fetched 2026-11-11. Wikipedia on the eruption: 'its precise date is of high importance and has been fiercely debated ... without coming to a definite conclusion.' I read only the Crossref abstract of Marinatos 1939, which is about the destruction of Minoan palaces; the Atlantis link is made by later writers (Atlantipedia lists Marinatos 1939 under 'Minoan Crete'). Galanopoulos and Luce books not read; named from Atlantipedia's chronology and Wikipedia's Atlantis article. Standing: I would keep 'plausible' but only for the inspiration claim.

hypotheses.name: Minoan Crete (Knossos)

proposed_by.work: The Critias and Minoan Crete, Journal of Hellenic Studies 33

hypotheses.argument: Frost argued that the Critias keeps a memory of Minoan Crete and treated Atlantis as a puzzle that a review of the whole Atlantis problem and of Solon's visit to Egypt could solve. Later writers added the sea power, the palace at Knossos and the bull imagery.

conflicts.how: Crete lies inside the Mediterranean and never sank (our legends.json 'against' note).
Minoan civilisation is a Bronze Age culture, and the eruption that hit it is dated about 1600 BCE (Wikipedia, Minoan eruption), nowhere near 9,600 BCE.

hypotheses.standing_reason: Treated as a possible source of the story's atmosphere by some classicists, never as a location; most scholars take the story as Plato's invention (National Geographic).

Atlantipedia's chronology lists 'K.T. Frost 1909 Minoans'; I did not see the 1909 text. Standing kept at 'plausible' on that thin basis.

proposed_by.work: Submergence and uplift of settlements in the area of Helike, Greece, Geoarchaeology 26
Documentary and web page

hypotheses.argument: The Greek city of Helike was destroyed by an earthquake and sea wave in winter 373 BCE, within Plato's lifetime. The Helike Project argues this recent disaster, not an ancient one, supplied the image of a city lost in a night.

tests.evidence: A Classical site 130m away, buried under 3m of similar sediments, may have been destroyed by the earthquake and tsunami of 373 B.C.

hypotheses.standing_reason: The destruction is well documented and the Helike Project and the BBC present it as the likely seed; this is the view of those researchers, not a consensus among classicists.

hypotheses.name: Spartel Bank

proposed_by.work: L'Atlantide devant le détroit de Gibraltar ? Mythe et géologie, Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences IIA 333
L'Atlantide retrouvée ? Enquête scientifique autour d'un mythe (Belin)

proposed_by.who: Georgeos Díaz-Montexano (disputes that Collina-Girard was first)
proposed_by.work: Magazine articles, Más Allá de la Ciencia, April 2000

hypotheses.argument: At the low sea level of the last ice age, Spartel Bank was an island west of the Strait of Gibraltar. Collina-Girard argues it was drowned by rising seas as the ice melted, around 11,000 to 12,000 years ago, and that Egyptian memory of this reached Plato.

fits.how: Spartel is just outside the Strait of Gibraltar, on the Atlantic side.
Sea-level rise drowned the island's top about 11,600 years ago, close to Plato's 9,000 years before Solon.
Gutscher tested whether a great earthquake and tsunami like Lisbon 1755 could have destroyed it.

conflicts.how: The mapped island is small; Gutscher estimated it at less than 500 m across at the time of the drowning (as reported in a 2005 Nature news piece reposted on Free Republic; original not fetched).

The same report says Gutscher's survey showed no unusual geometric structures; Wikipedia adds that in follow-up correspondence he said the island could not have supported the Bronze Age society Plato describes.

tests.what: High-resolution bathymetry of Spartel and a tsunami hazard analysis
tests.result: The morphology of the paleoisland was mapped and the viability of habitation discussed. A great earthquake and tsunami are plausible for the Gulf of Cádiz, but Gutscher later said the island could not have held Plato's Bronze Age city.
tests.evidence: The detailed morphology of Spartel paleoisland, as determined from recently acquired high-resolution bathymetric data, is reported here.

replies.who: Heinz-Günther Nesselrath, Bryn Mawr Classical Review
replies.what: Collina-Girard has shed light on prehistory west of Gibraltar but 'just as certainly, however, he has not found Plato's Atlantis'; the review also calls his knowledge of Plato derivative and notes inaccuracies.
Each says the other's version is pseudoscience (Wikipedia, Atlantis).

hypotheses.standing_reason: The island is real, but its main geological analyst (Gutscher) and the classicist reviewer (Nesselrath) both say it is not Plato's Atlantis.
hypotheses.date_of_the_proposed_event: about 9,600 BCE to 9,400 BCE (about 11,600 years ago)
hypotheses.notes: Wikidata Q2881958 ("Spartel") property P625, fetched 2026-11-11. Collina-Girard 2001 abstract not available to me (Crossref and Semantic Scholar have none); his case is taken from the BMCR review and Gutscher's abstract. Depth -56 m is the BMCR review's 'now about 55 m below sea-level' rounded; I kept the globe's -56. The 500 m figure rests on a forum repost of Nature news, so low reliability. Coordinates: Wikidata Q2881958 (see build step). Standing: I would keep 'rejected', with the note that Collina-Girard still defends it. Position moved 2026-11-11 to the bank's shallowest point in two open depth grids (GMRT 50 m and EMODnet 100 m agree within 150 m: 35.9036 N, 5.9615 W, about 72 m down). The plain from the south coast to Seville, with the Sierra Morena and Sierra Nevada as the mountains (Kühne).

The site does not match Plato's size, rings or date, and the project was hijacked for a Biblical agenda.

hypotheses.name: Richat Structure (Eye of the Sahara)

proposed_by.who: Online videos and books from about 2018 (for example Charles Giuliani's book on the Richat as Atlantis)
proposed_by.work: popular videos and a book; the earliest publication was not traced

hypotheses.argument: The Richat Structure is a 40 km circular feature of concentric ridges. Promoters say its rings match the alternating rings of land and water around Plato's city.

fits.how: Promoters note concentric rings; the structure has three nested rings by Matton et al.'s description (a geological fact, not a claim of Atlantis).

conflicts.how: It lies deep in the Sahara, inland from the Atlantic coast, not in front of the Pillars (our legends.json 'against' note).
The rings are rock ridges eroded from a dome; there is no sign of dug canals or a built city, and no midden or buildings were found (Wikipedia, Richat Structure).

tests.what: Geological study of the structure
tests.result: It is the eroded top of a Cretaceous alkaline complex with a hydrothermal karst breccia core, formed by doming and erosion over millions of years.
tests.evidence: The circular Richat structure and its breccia core thus represent the superficial expression of a Cretaceous alkaline complex with an exceptionally well preserved hydrothermal karst infilling at its summit.

tests.what: Archaeological survey of the structure's depressions
tests.who: Prehistoric artefact mapping from 1974 onward (as summarised by Wikipedia)
tests.result: Acheulean stone tools along the wadis and sparse Neolithic points; no settlement debris.
tests.evidence: The Richat Structure is the location of exceptional accumulations of Acheulean artifacts.

replies.what: Describes the structure as an uplifted geologic dome initially mistaken for an impact structure.

hypotheses.standing_reason: Promoted outside scholarship; geology and archaeology done for other reasons exclude a built city, but nobody has tested the Atlantis claim directly.
hypotheses.date_of_the_proposed_event: about 9,600 BCE; the dome itself is Cretaceous

sources.title: Geographical, The Eye of the Sahara

I would keep 'fringe' rather than 'rejected': the geology and tool surveys were not designed to test Atlantis, though they exclude a city. hypotheses.name: Azores Plateau and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge

proposed_by.work: Atlantis: The Antediluvian World
Lecture on a recent sinking north of the Azores

hypotheses.argument: Donnelly argued that the Azores are the peaks of the sunken continent. He says black lava and red and white rock on the Azores match Plato's three stones and that the Azores have hot springs, and read the surrounding peaks as the mountains that sheltered the plain.

fits.how: Donnelly: 'upon the Azores black lava rocks, and rocks red and white in color, are now found.'
Donnelly: 'hot springs abound in the Azores, which are the surviving fragments of Atlantis.'
Donnelly: the surrounding mountains 'are represented in the present towering peaks of the Azores.'
The Azores lie in the open Atlantic, about 1,400 km west of Portugal.

tests.evidence: that the Azores are volcanic islands and are not the remnants of a more or less large continental mass, for they are not composed of rocks seen on the continents (as quoted by Wikipedia from Schuchert)

replies.what: Replied to Termier's lecture and to Atlantis claims with the geology above.

hypotheses.standing_reason: Examined by geologists a century ago and since; the sea floor has been deep for millions of years.

hypotheses.name: Bimini Road

The Stones of Atlantis (Prentice-Hall)

tests.what: Attempted decipherment of Maya glyphs by Brasseur and Le Plongeon
tests.result: Atlantipedia says the efforts to link Latin with Mayan glyphs and the de Landa alphabet 'bore little fruit'.
tests.evidence: Both Donnelly's efforts to link Latin with Mayan glyphs and deLanda's attempt to identify the Mayan alphabet bore little fruit

replies.what: Brasseur is significant today primarily for discovering and publishing colonial sources on the Maya, including the Troano Codex, not for his Atlantis reading.

hypotheses.standing_reason: The decipherments failed and the Maya script was later read as a record of Maya language and history; this is the verdict of epigraphers and of the reference sources above.
hypotheses.notes: Wikidata Q130978 ("Yucatan Peninsula") property P625, fetched 2026-11-11. Wikipedia on Donnelly: much of his writing 'was inspired by the publications of Charles Étienne Brasseur de Bourbourg and the fieldwork of Augustus Le Plongeon in the Yucatan'. Atlantipedia's chronology lists Brasseur in 1850 under 'Hispaniola', which conflicts with the 1868 date from the search summary; I left the proposal date vague. I did not read their books. No fits or conflicts tagged for lack of a source tying them to specific claims.

hypotheses.name: Sundaland and Indonesia

proposed_by.work: Atlantis: The Lost Continent Finally Found: The Definitive Localization of Plato's Lost Continent
Plato Never Lied: Atlantis Is In Indonesia (Kindle ebook, as listed by Wikipedia)

hypotheses.argument: Santos, a Brazilian physicist, argued that Atlantis was Sundaland, the shelf of South-East Asia that flooded at the end of the last ice age, and that Plato's Pillars of Heracles are the volcanoes Krakatau and Dempo. Natawidjaja, an Indonesian geologist, has argued a related case.

fits.how: Sundaland's shelf was dry land during the ice age and drowned as the ice melted (Atlantipedia on Indonesia).

conflicts.how: Santos redefines the Pillars of Heracles as the Krakatau and Dempo mountains in the Sunda Strait, against the Greek-usage of Gibraltar.

hypotheses.standing_reason: Promoted by Santos's followers and a few Indonesian scientists; no classicists or archaeologists in the sources I found endorse it.
hypotheses.date_of_the_proposed_event: the end of the last ice age, about 11,000 to 20,000 years ago

sources.title: The Jakarta Post, Indonesia: The lost Atlantis? (2010)

hypotheses.notes: Wikidata Q2366175 ("Sundaland") property P625, fetched 2026-11-11. I read the Jakarta Post feature and Atlantipedia's Indonesia entry. The Jakarta Post also quotes the chairman of the Indonesian Institute of Sciences saying scientists have found a big island beneath the South China Sea that sank during the Pleistocene ice age; this is the closest I found to a geoscience statement. Natawidjaja's separate claim about the Gunung Padang site was published and then retracted in March 2024 (Wikipedia), and I found no source tying that site to Atlantis, so it is not a pin. The Santos book year is not shown in what I fetched. Reports of the Indonesian archaeologist Daud Tanudirjo calling the idea 'premature' appeared in a search summary only and were not verified.

hypotheses.name: The Arctic and Spitsbergen (Bailly)

proposed_by.work: Lettres sur l'Atlantide de Platon et sur l'ancienne histoire de l'Asie

hypotheses.argument: Bailly, an astronomer, proposed that Spitsbergen was the site of Hyperborea and Atlantis and that Atlantis was the root civilisation that civilised the Chinese, Indians and Egyptians. He met the problem of Plato's elephants by saying the Arctic was warmer in ancient times.

fits.how: Bailly proposed the Arctic once had a warmer climate, to allow large animals.

conflicts.how: Spitsbergen is not in front of the Pillars.

hypotheses.standing_reason: An 18th-century reading overtaken by later climate and ice-core science; no modern scholar defends it.
hypotheses.notes: Wikidata Q21162 ("Spitsbergen") property P625, fetched 2026-11-11. Atlantipedia notes an idea 'incorrectly thought by some to have been supported by Voltaire' and that Bailly identified Iceland as Ogygia. Wikipedia lists the 1779 title as 'Discourse on Plato's Atlantide'. I did not read the French scan on the Internet Archive that a search surfaced.

hypotheses.name: The North Pole (William F. Warren)

proposed_by.work: Paradise Found: The Cradle of the Human Race at the North Pole

hypotheses.argument: Warren, a professor of theology at Boston University, held that mankind began at the North Pole and placed Atlantis there, along with the Garden of Eden, Mount Meru, Avalon and Hyperborea.

conflicts.how: The pole is not in front of the Pillars.

hypotheses.standing_reason: A 19th-century theological geography; Wikipedia lists it among older proposals with no modern backing.
hypotheses.notes: Wikidata Q934 ("North Pole") property P625, fetched 2026-11-11. One secondary source only; Warren's book was not read.

hypotheses.name: The Holy Land, Israel and Sinai

proposed_by.work: listed by Atlantipedia as the first to place Atlantis in the Holy Land
Book placing Atlantis in the Holy Land
Modern claim: Israel with the Sinai Peninsula as Atlantis

hypotheses.argument: From the 16th to the 18th century, several scholars took Plato's story as a garbled account of early Jewish history, with the Promised Land as Atlantis. A modern writer, Jaime Manuschevich, identifies Israel with Sinai as the site.

conflicts.how: The Levant is at the eastern end of the Mediterranean.

replies.who: Atlantisforschung, quoted by Atlantipedia on Van Eys
replies.what: 'the heyday of the Atlantis in the Holy Land thesis was already over' by 1827, a short-lived renaissance of an outdated Bible-true view.

hypotheses.standing_reason: A Bible-based reading abandoned by scholars in the 18th century; the modern version is argued outside scholarship.
hypotheses.notes: Wikidata Q801 ("Israel") property P625, fetched 2026-11-11. Atlantipedia also lists Gerardus Vossius, Pierre-Daniel Huet and Johann Albert Fabricius in its chronology as Holy Land readers; I did not read any of their works. Ryan Pitterson (Golan Heights, Judgement of the Nephilim) is mentioned there as a modern claim; the Golan has concentric stone walls at Gilgal Refaim.

hypotheses.name: Cádiz (Gadir) and its bay

proposed_by.work: Wrote a history of Cádiz suggesting Atlantis extended from Cádiz to Malta
Expedition to search for Atlantis off Cádiz

hypotheses.argument: Plato names the king of the island's tip Gadeiros, twin of Atlas, a name Atlantipedia links to Gades (Cádiz). Asher led an expedition off the coast in 1973 and announced a find of Plato's island.

fits.how: Cádiz is accepted as ancient Gades, considered the kingdom of Gadeirus, twin brother of Atlas.

tests.what: Expedition off Cádiz
tests.result: Despite claims of having discovered Plato's island, nothing verifiable was found.
tests.evidence: despite claims of having discovered Plato's Island, nothing verifiable was found

hypotheses.standing_reason: The place-name link is old, but the 1973 expedition found nothing verifiable; this is Atlantipedia's account.
hypotheses.notes: Wikidata Q15682 ("Cádiz") property P625, fetched 2026-11-11. The 2022 Seville claim to have found the Temple of Hercules Gaditanus in the Bay of Cádiz, mentioned on the same page, is about a different question (the Phoenician temple) and is not an Atlantis claim.

hypotheses.name: Greenland and the north Atlantic (La Mothe le Vayer to Dantas)

proposed_by.who: François de La Mothe le Vayer
proposed_by.work: 17th-century writer, the first to propose Greenland (Atlantipedia)
Paper submitted to the 2008 Atlantis Conference, Athens

hypotheses.argument: Greenland was first proposed in the 17th century. Modern authors compare its outline with Athanasius Kircher's map of Atlantis, or propose the Baffin Basin to its west as the plain.

conflicts.how: Atlantipedia notes Kircher's map places Atlantis between the Strait of Gibraltar and America, not between Canada and Scandinavia.

hypotheses.standing_reason: A few authors compare maps; no field or survey work is cited.
hypotheses.notes: Wikidata Q223 ("Greenland") property P625, fetched 2026-11-11. Atlantipedia's entry is an editor's survey and mentions Dale Huffman, Johan Nygren, Riaan Booysen and Ian Fox (Baffin Basin); I read only that entry.

handoffs.what: Spartel Bank: Gutscher's 2005 high-resolution bathymetry is the one survey made to test an Atlantis claim; find open multibeam and load at a sea level near -60 m (sources.json: emodnet-bathymetry-multicolour, gmrt-wms).

Dogger Bank, Heligoland, Little Sole Bank, Le Danois Bank and the Cyprus Basin all sit on open EMODnet bathymetry; Doñana and Souss-Massa need land DEM or lidar (sources.json: spain-pnoa-lidar-dsm, copernicus-dem-aws).
Richat: Matton et al. 2005 geology and the Acheulean artefact surveys are the tests; macrostrat-geology and copernicus-dem-aws can show the dome and rings.

Claims that were announced and then not followed by a published survey: Sarmast (Cyprus, 2004), Zelitsky (Cuba, 2001), Asher (Cádiz, 1973), Koudriavtsev (Little Sole Bank, planned 1998), Spanuth's 1952 dive (Heligoland), Freund (Doñana, 2011), Los Atlantes (Lanzarote, 2024).

Several proposers change Plato's numbers or terms: Herrmann cuts the dimensions by 30 (schoinos versus stade), Kühne uses a stade 20% longer, Zangger and James treat the Egyptian source as distorted, Schoppe and Santos and Frau move the Pillars. Please record the Greek for 'Atlantic', 'Pillars' and the length units.
Claim ids from the brief were enough for me. Only 'ten-kings' ties to a place name (Gadeiros and Cádiz, per Atlantipedia); please confirm the Greek for that link.

Proposals need sea level and coastlines at several dates: about 9,600 BCE (Spartel, Antarctica, Azov), about 6,200 BCE (Doggerland, Storegga), about 5,500 BCE (Black Sea and Bosporus), about 3,100 BCE (Dunbavin) and about 1,200 BCE (Heligoland, Sardinia). Sundaland needs its own shelf flooding dates.

not_verified: Mid-Atlantic Ridge sediment-core 'test' (Pettersson's 1947 to 1948 Albatross expedition, freshwater diatoms): a search found the cores and the diatom literature but nothing tying them to Atlantis, so it is not used.

Great Meteor Seamount, Gorringe Bank, Ampere Seamount, Rockall and the Faroe area: no published Atlantis proposal found. The Marine Regions gazetteer lists an 'Atlantis-Great Meteor Seamount Chain' (a name for the feature, not a proposal). A claim that Heezen and others (1954) suggested the Atlantis seamount was an island in the last 12,000 years appeared only on a fringe site and is not used.

Finland, India and Sri Lanka, South China Sea, Brazil, Denmark: not included. Atlantipedia's entries mention Hancock's Underworld and a Gulf of Cambay article, a Tamil Kumari Kandam tradition, a few Brazilian claims and a Catalan Wikipedia note with no authority, but I found no work that proposes Atlantis there and that I could cite. The Jakarta Post quotes the head of LIPI on a sunken island under the South China Sea, which is cited under Sundaland only.

Strait of Sicily: Atlantipedia lists John Borg (1910), and a search surfaced 'A scientific approach to Plato's Atlantis' (Atti della Accademia Peloritana dei Pericolanti) and a preprint by Massimo Rapisarda. The journal and preprint pages did not load for me, so there is no pin. Sergio Frau's Sardinia case rests on the Strait of Sicily being the Pillars.
